refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7543-7546 verbatim: "The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing)." All three examples are defects of the request message itself, matching the claim's "in the request itself".

refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7589-7591 verbatim: "The 404 (Not Found) status code indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists." The claim reproduces both halves. The sentence that follows (7591-7594, the 410 preference) is not touched by the lesson.

refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7652-7654 verbatim: "The 409 (Conflict) status code indicates that the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource." The section continues "This code is used in situations where the user might be able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request" — consistent with §4's shipped-order framing, which the lesson keeps hypothetical.

DonHang.Domain/IOrderRepository.cs @ stage-1: `Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id);`. Sole implementation EfOrderRepository uses `.FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id)`, which yields null for no match rather than throwing. Live this round: authenticated `PATCH /api/v1/orders/-5/cancel` -> 404 `{"title":"Not found","status":404,"detail":"order -5 not found"}` — the null became KeyNotFoundException, not a 500, which is what §4's "still `404` in this app, not `400`" rests on.

Still no rfc9457 mirror under refs/rfc (only 6265/9110/9111/9112), so fetched again from www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457 this round. §3.1 introduces the list as "Problem detail objects can have the following members. If a member's value type does not match the specified type, the member MUST be ignored." and defines title/status/detail as quoted there. No sentence declaring the members optional was returned; "can have" is the strongest wording actually seen, so "none mandated" is an inference, not a quote.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: RFC 9457 §3.1: "Problem detail objects can have the following members" — type, status, title, detail, instance; none is stated as required. Đơn Hàng's WriteProblemAsync fills exactly title/status/detail, this app's choice, not a requirement of the format.

claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:db/schema.sql line 23: `CHECK (status IN ('new', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled'))` — exactly these four values. db/seed.sql:24-35 uses 'new', 'paid' and 'shipped'; 'cancelled' is produced by CancelOrderAsync. This anchors §4's reworded "Every order carries its own `Status` — `"new"`, `"paid"`, `"shipped"`, or `"cancelled"`", which no longer implies a sequence.

issues.text: The clause added this round gets the mechanism half right. ExceptionHandlingMiddleware does supply both fields — `WriteProblemAsync(context, StatusCodes.Status404NotFound, "Not found", ex.Message)` — but the title is a literal picked per exception type alongside the status code, not derived from it; the wording invites the reader to expect a generic 404 -> "Not found" mapping. No ledger claim covers where title/status come from (claim 3 covers only the body as a whole).
issues.quote: it fills `title` and `status` itself from the status code it picked, so only `detail` comes from the exception
issues.fix: Drop the causal phrase: "— it supplies `title` and `status` itself, so only `detail` comes from the exception". Add a `fact` claim to .meta.json with source_hint "examples/don-hang @ stage-1: DonHang.Api/Middleware/ExceptionHandlingMiddleware.cs — catch (KeyNotFoundException ex) => WriteProblemAsync(context, Status404NotFound, 'Not found', ex.Message)".

issues.text: The key (`c`) and the rewritten option `d` are both sound, but `b`'s explanation now contradicts `d`'s and misstates the class. RFC 9110 §15.5 (refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7534-7535): "The 4xx (Client Error) class of status code indicates that the client seems to have erred." So 4xx does say who erred — exactly what `d`'s explanation asserts ("the server didn't do anything wrong in either case") — while `b`'s explanation says being 4xx "only means the client is expected to act differently before retrying".
issues.quote: Being in the same `4xx` class only means the client is expected to act differently before retrying — it says nothing about the two meaning the same specific thing.
issues.fix: Reword `b`'s explanation (en and vi) to concede the shared part and deny the rest: "Both being `4xx` does say the client is the one who erred — it just doesn't say the two errors are the same one: a broken request and a missing id are different failures."

issues.text: I read this paragraph twice and still had to guess. The picture shows one request walking A -> B -> D -> F, but boxes C and E name two different endpoints, so my first reading was that one request goes through `POST /api/v1/orders` and then `PATCH .../cancel`. The sentence meant to stop that is the hardest one in the lesson: I cannot tell what "them" points at. Box G also names no endpoint at all, so "each name what illustrates them" is not even true of all three boxes.
issues.quote: not necessarily three checks inside one single endpoint; the diagram's three status boxes each name what illustrates them
issues.fix: Replace that clause with two plain sentences: "The three boxes are not stages of one request. The `400` box names the endpoint that illustrates it, `POST /api/v1/orders`; the `404` box names `PATCH .../cancel`; the `409` box names a check this app does not have." Then start a new paragraph at "First: is the request itself broken?".

issues.text: "a valid token" is a term I have never met — not in what I already know, and the lesson never says what a token is or why sending one changes the answer. It sits in the paragraph that is supposed to set the scene, and it made me stop to wonder whether an invalid token has its own status code, which the lesson never answers. I only learn a token is something I fetch by logging in when I reach Try it, five sections later.
issues.quote: Sending `PATCH /api/v1/orders/99999/cancel`, with a valid token, gets `404`
issues.fix: Keep the condition but point at where it is handled: replace "with a valid token" with "(signed in, as in Try it below)".

issues.text: "route" is a word I do not know. I know `endpoint` — a method-and-path pair mapped to handler code — and I think that is what is meant, but I cannot be sure, and the whole sentence turns on it: it is the condition that separates a `404` from whatever happens otherwise.
issues.quote: as long as it's a value the route accepts, a lookup that finds nothing is still `404` in this app, not `400`
issues.fix: Replace "the route" with "the endpoint" (a term I already know); this is the only place the word appears.

issues.text: "as long as it's a value the endpoint accepts" tells me some ids are not accepted, and I immediately wanted to know what `PATCH /api/v1/orders/abc/cancel` answers. The lesson never says, and it has just told me this endpoint has "nothing to be malformed", so I am left guessing between `400`, `404` and something else.
issues.quote: This holds even when the id itself looks like an obviously wrong number
issues.fix: After "not `400`", add one scoping clause: "An id the endpoint cannot read as a number never reaches the method at all, so it is outside these three questions."

issues.text: The prose walks all three questions but never mentions the `no` arrow out of "does its state conflict?" or the `succeeds` box, so one node of the picture is left for me to narrate alone. issues.fix: End the third paragraph of "How it works" with one sentence: "If nothing conflicts, the cancel goes through — that's the `succeeds` box."

issues.text: I am told where `detail` comes from (the exception's own message) but not where `title` and `status` come from. Both §2 and §7 show me `"title":"Not found"`, and after this sentence I would have guessed the exception carries that text too — the code block shows it does not.

issues.text: `status` means two different things in code font a few lines apart: the Problem Details field (`"status":404`, named in Core concepts) and the order's own field. On first read of "Every order carries a `status`" I thought an order carried a response status code, and only §5's `order.Status` sorted me out.
